How many times have you promised yourself to go to the gym? Or eat healthy? Or save money?
The truth is that we are all bad at changing. How can we acquire good habits according to science?

behavior, and reward. For example: hunger is our trigger, we seek food
(that is the behavior) and we get the reward of satisfying our hunger. The problem
is when a habit – or the lack of one – causes disorders in health or in our relationships
and prevents us from living happily or achieving our goals. But changing habits is not that easy!
There are many books and life coaches out there telling you how to change, the problem is that
they don't seem to agree. Some say: “A big change will make you see immediate results
and motivate you,” while others say: “Small changes will be easier to maintain,
you'll see long-term results, but they will be lasting.” Some tell you: “Have a clear goal
and work to achieve it and without realizing it, you'll create a habit,” while others say: “Don't focus on the
goal but on changing the system.” “Set a schedule,” “Don't set a schedule.” Oh! It seems
impossible, especially when they tell you that you need the mysterious and elusive: “willpower.”
A few years ago, some researchers decided it would be fun to torture 4-year-olds and devised: “the marshmallow experiment.” They were placed in front of a marshmallow and told that
they would be left alone for a moment; if they didn't eat the marshmallow, they could eat that marshmallow and another one,
but if they ate it, they wouldn't get an extra marshmallow. Ten minutes later, only a third of
the children managed to resist. One girl even tried to eat just the inside to pretend she
hadn't eaten it. Years later, it was observed that the children who had managed to resist
were more successful than those who gave in to temptation. This characteristic was called
“delayed gratification.” It seems that willpower is beneficial in our lives.
But how does it work? One of the most famous experiments in this area is by Roy Baumeister.
Now, to torture adults, a group of people was asked not to eat anything for three hours,
then they were taken to a room with two bowls: one contained radishes, the other
freshly baked chocolate cookies and small chocolates. Some were only allowed to eat
radishes and others cookies (plus a control group that ate nothing). Afterwards,
everyone was asked to solve a mental puzzle that had no solution (scientists can really
be evil). Those who had eaten radishes gave up quickly, while
those who ate cookies persisted more than twice as long (though a little less than the
control group). The interpretation was that: those who had to use their willpower to
resist the cookies no longer had willpower left to work on the puzzle. It
was concluded that willpower was like a muscle that got fatigued, but it was also
possible to strengthen it over time. This theory is known as “Ego Depletion.” This theory was
accepted for a long time, but it turns out that it has now faced replicability issues. A study
found that people who believed in “ego depletion” showed a placebo effect and had
limited willpower. Today, there is no answer and we don't have much idea of how it works.
really the willpower. What we do know is that: the prefrontal cortex is responsible for
willpower, but since it is the area that evolved more recently, it is quite
weak and shuts down in situations of stress, sleep, or fear. Relying solely on our willpower
to curb our behavior is not very effective, plus socioeconomic
and emotional factors affect our willpower. But from the torture of infants, we learned that:
children who did not eat the marshmallow did everything possible not to think about it,
they avoided seeing it or played to think about something else. Using willpower to
change a habit is based on avoiding the behavior, but to not depend
on willpower, it is easier to avoid the trigger. If you want to avoid social media
during your work hours, use an app to block them. Want to stop eating sugar?
avoid that aisle. It is more efficient to avoid contact with temptation than to resist it.
When it is not possible to avoid the trigger and we find it hard to avoid the behavior, we can
change the reward. Not all your actions become habits; your brain decides what to turn
into a habit and what not based on the reward obtained. Unfortunately, it is our primitive brain
or monkey mind that usually scores people, places, and things. Our
primitive mind only cares about surviving long enough to reproduce, it doesn't think much about
the future and likes immediate rewards. It is not surprising that it prefers foods
higher in fat and sugar, even though they are no longer synonymous with survival but with slow death.
The habit is maintained or grows when we continue to associate the reward with good things. But
if Skinner taught pigeons to play ping pong just for a reward, we can also
use this system to our advantage. Psychiatrist and neuroscientist Judson Brewer has
found a solution in mindful meditation. The default neural network
or our “monkey mind” is the one that is active during the formation and maintenance of habits,
mindful meditation reduces the activity of this network. After a bit of training,
the doctor asks his patients that the next time they repeat the bad habit they want to change,
they observe their sensations and emotions as if meditating and ask themselves with curiosity:
What do I feel while doing it? Do I really have a reward now? It sounds strange, but this
modifies the reward scale and has managed to change the habits of smokers, who
eat out of anxiety and have high levels of stress. It is also possible to change the reward for
habits we would like to form. To an unpleasant activity or one that you simply forget, you can
add a reward, although you have to be creative to avoid: “as a reward for
exercising, a chocolate!”. You can listen to your favorite podcast only when you exercise,
have a cup of coffee while working and not as an excuse to take a break or watch a
movie after studying. This is known as: the “Premack Principle”: a pleasant and frequent behavior reinforces a less pleasant or infrequent behavior, as long as the
pleasant behavior is done after the other. Also, when you are waiting for something you like,
the mere expectation releases dopamine and this can be associated with the habit you want to form.
Do you need to set a schedule and place for your new habit? Google workers
were incentivized to exercise in exchange for a monetary reward. Some were only
allowed to go at a time they had chosen themselves, while others were given
total freedom of schedule. Who do you think exercised more? Contrary to what one might expect,
those without a schedule exercised more. While it's a good idea to have a schedule and a place,
life is unpredictable and the ability to be flexible allows us to adapt better.
Creating or breaking a habit requires consistency and flexibility, but above
all, it needs to be a conscious and introspective change. Ask yourself: What could go wrong?
Why have you failed before? Perhaps you can reduce or add friction as needed. For
example: have everything ready to exercise the next day or turn off the TV. You can
have some method to track your progress. Or if you feel very tired, just try your habit halfway,
just think about putting on workout clothes and stretching for two minutes; maybe that will be enough to
motivate you. Think of a method that works for you and try again. But above all, think
why do you want to change? We are constantly bombarded with information: eat five different fruits,
an apple, nuts, and something green, drink two liters of water, three cups of tea,
sunbathe for fifteen minutes, listen to inspiring songs, read, dance, learn to play
an instrument, do an hour of exercise, clean and organize, talk to your loved ones,
give five hugs and do that every day. While it could bring us benefits, it's impossible to change
everything overnight, and sometimes there's not enough time. Think about how much others influence
both your good and bad habits and which ones you would really like to change. Interestingly!
